# Book I, Proposition 6

*Equal base angles make equal sides*

> If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/06.svg" alt="The figure for Proposition I.6" width="360"></p>

## Euclid's proof

Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;

I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.

For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.

Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;

let DC be joined.

Then, since DB is equal to AC,

and BC is common,

the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;

and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;

therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,

and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,

the less to the greater:

which is absurd.

Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;

it is therefore equal to it.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop06.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop06.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- What Euclid sees in the figure but never says: `D`, cut off on `BA`, is not on
the straight line `BC`, so `DBC` is a triangle (and I.4 may be applied to it). -/
theorem Prop6.figure {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBDA : Between B D A) :
    Triangle B D C := by
  rintro ⟨L, hB, hD, hC⟩
  /- A straight line through B and D goes on through A, and then A, B, C would
     lie on one straight line. -/
  exact hABC ⟨L, on_line_of_between hBDA hB hD, hB, hC⟩

/-- The triangle `ABC`, named from another corner, as `CAB`. -/
theorem Prop6.rotate {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) : Triangle C A B := by
  rintro ⟨L, hC, hA, hB⟩
  exact hABC ⟨L, hA, hB, hC⟩

/-- The triangle `ABC`, named the other way round, as `ACB`. -/
theorem Prop6.swap {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) : Triangle A C B := by
  rintro ⟨L, hA, hC, hB⟩
  exact hABC ⟨L, hA, hB, hC⟩

/-- What Euclid sees in the figure: `D` lies on `BA`, on the same side of `B` as
`A`, so the angle `DBC` is the angle `ABC` itself (System E, Diagram-angle 4). -/
theorem Prop6.angle {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBDA : Between B D A) :
    ∠ D B C = ∠ A B C := by
  obtain ⟨BA, hB_BA, hA_BA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hABC.ne₂₃
  exact angle_eq_of_same_rays hB_BA (on_line_of_between_ends hBDA hB_BA hA_BA) hA_BA
    hB_BC hC_BC hC_BC (ne_of_between hBDA).symm hABC.ne₁₂ hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm
    (not_between_of_between hBDA) (fun h => ne_of_between_ends h rfl)

/-- The tacit assumption Heath points out: because `D` is between `A` and `B`, the
triangle `DBC` is less than the triangle `ACB`. The straight line `CD` cuts `ACB`
into `DBC` and `ADC` (System E, Diagram-area 2), `ADC` is something, since `C` is
not on `AB` (Diagram-area 1), and the whole is greater than the part (C.N. 5). -/
theorem Prop6.less {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBDA : Between B D A) :
    △ D B C < △ A C B := by
  obtain ⟨BA, hB, hA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hD : OnLine D BA := on_line_of_between_ends hBDA hB hA
  have hC : ¬ OnLine C BA := fun hC => hABC ⟨BA, hA, hB, hC⟩
  have hDA : D ≠ A := (ne_of_between (between_symm hBDA)).symm
  /- The two parts make up the whole. -/
  have hwhole : △ B D C + △ C D A = △ B C A :=
    area_add_of_between hB hA hD hABC.ne₁₂.symm (ne_of_between hBDA) hDA.symm hC hBDA
  /- The part ADC is something: a triangle with no area would have C on BA. -/
  have hpart : △ C D A ≠ 0 := by
    intro h0
    rw [← area_rotate D A C] at h0
    exact hC (on_line_of_area_eq_zero hD hA hDA h0)
  have := CommonNotion5 (a := △ B D C) (Magnitude.pos_of_ne_zero hpart)
  rw [hwhole, area_rotate B C A, area_swap A B C, ← area_rotate D C B, ← area_swap D B C]
    at this
  exact this

/-- If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles
will also be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop6 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;
  -- I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.
  -- For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.
  /- That of two unequal lengths one is the greater is a tacit law of
     magnitudes (System E §3.5), `lt_trichotomy`. -/
  have one_greater : ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ → ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
    intro hne
    rcases lt_trichotomy ‖A B‖ ‖A C‖ with hlt | heq | hgt
    · exact Or.inr hlt
    · exact absurd heq hne
    · exact Or.inl hgt
  /- Euclid takes AB to be the greater. The other case is his argument again
     with B and C exchanged, so we give the argument for every triangle whose
     angles at B and C are equal, and use it twice below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B →
      ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ → False := by
    intro B C hABC h hAC_AB
    -- Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;
    /- Euclid gives no reference, but cutting off is I.3, from the end B. -/
    have hAC_BA : ‖A C‖ < ‖B A‖ := by rw [len_symm B A]; exact hAC_AB
    obtain ⟨D, hBDA, hBD⟩ := Prop3 (A := B) (B := A) hABC.ne₁₃ hAC_BA
    -- let DC be joined.
    /- Lean needs only the points D and C; the straight line DC is drawn for
       the eye. -/
    -- Then, since DB is equal to AC,
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖A C‖ := (len_symm D B).trans hBD
    -- and BC is common,
    have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
    -- the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;
    have hsides : ‖B D‖ = ‖C A‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
      ⟨(len_symm B D).trans (hDB.trans (len_symm A C)), hBC⟩
    -- and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;
    /- The angle DBC is the angle ABC itself, since D lies on BA
       (`Prop6.angle`), and ABC is equal to ACB by hypothesis. -/
    have hDBC : ∠ D B C = ∠ A C B := (Prop6.angle hABC hBDA).trans h
    -- therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,
    /- This is I.4, applied to the triangles DBC and ACB; that DBC is a
       triangle at all is `Prop6.figure`. -/
    obtain ⟨hDC_AB, hBDC_CAB, -, -⟩ :=
      Prop4 (Prop6.figure hABC hBDA) (Prop6.rotate hABC) hsides.1 hsides.2 hDBC
    -- and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,
    have hequal : △ D B C = △ A C B := by
      rw [area_swap D B C, area_rotate D C B, hBDC_CAB, ← area_rotate A B C, area_swap A B C]
    -- the less to the greater:
    /- Heath: "Euclid assumes that, because D is between A and B, the
       triangle DBC is less than the triangle ABC." Lean makes us prove it:
       `Prop6.less`. -/
    have hless : △ D B C < △ A C B := Prop6.less hABC hBDA
    -- which is absurd.
    rw [hequal] at hless
    exact lt_irrefl _ hless
  -- Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;
  have hnot : ¬ ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ := fun hne =>
    (one_greater hne).elim (greater hABC h) (greater (Prop6.swap hABC) h.symm)
  -- it is therefore equal to it.
  /- Reductio ad absurdum: a length not unequal to another is equal to it. -/
  exact Classical.byContradiction hnot
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**The first reductio.** "We have here used, for the first time in the *Elements*, the method of *reductio ad absurdum*," Heath notes (vol. 1, p. 256). Euclid supposes AB greater than AC and lets the figure contradict itself. Both ends of the argument are rules of reasoning rather than geometry. "If AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater" is the tacit law of magnitudes `lt_trichotomy` (System E §3.5), and the last step, from "not unequal" to "equal", is Lean's `Classical.byContradiction`.

**The less and the greater.** Heath again: "Euclid assumes that, because D is between A and B, the triangle DBC is less than the triangle ABC. Some postulate is necessary to justify this tacit assumption" (vol. 1, p. 256). Here it is `Prop6.less`, and it comes from three rules. The straight line CD cuts the triangle into DBC and ADC (`area_add_of_between`, System E's Diagram-area 2); ADC has some area, because C is not on AB (`on_line_of_area_eq_zero`, Diagram-area 1); and the whole is greater than the part (Common Notion 5). Avigad, Dean and Mumma wrote those area rules for moments like this one, and Michael Beeson, Julien Narboux and Freek Wiedijk, checking Book I by machine, likewise found that Euclid's "equal figures" need axioms of their own.

**What else the figure says.** Two more facts are read off the picture. DBC is a triangle at all, so I.4 may be applied to it (`Prop6.figure`), and the angle DBC is the angle ABC itself, because D lies on BA (`Prop6.angle`, from Diagram-angle 4). Euclid treats only the case in which AB is the greater. The other case is the same with B and C exchanged, so the Lean gives the argument once, for any triangle with equal angles at the base, and uses it both ways round. And the base DC, which Euclid proves equal to AB and then never uses, is simply the first thing I.4 hands back.

**A converse.** I.6 turns the first part of I.5 around. Heath, following Proclus, calls this the "leading" kind of conversion, in which hypothesis and conclusion change places exactly, and adds that "I. 6 is the geometrical, but not the logical, converse of I. 5" (vol. 1, p. 256). De Morgan observed that I.6 is "a purely logical deduction from I. 5 and I. 18 taken together", and Todhunter that it "could be postponed till later and proved by means of I. 26" (vol. 1, pp. 256, 258). The proof above keeps to Euclid's own route, through I.3, I.4 and the part that is less than the whole.

**The modern way.** Put B at (−1, 0), C at (1, 0) and A at (x, y). Equal angles at B and C make the slopes of BA and CA equal and opposite, y/(x + 1) = y/(1 − x), so x = 0: A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, and AB = AC = √(1 + y²).
